name: Overthinking Test
tagline: Discover where your thoughts get stuck and how to unwind them.
intro: This test explores four common patterns of overthinking: dwelling on the past, worrying about the future, struggling with decisions and replaying social moments. Answer based on how often each statement fits you in daily life. It takes about five minutes and shows you which thinking loops take up most of your mental energy.
seoTitle: Overthinking Test: Free online overthinking check
seoDescription: Do you overthink everything? Take this 5-minute test on rumination, worry, indecision and social replay and get practical tips to quiet your mind.

rumination.name: Rumination
rumination.short: How much you dwell on past events, mistakes and problems.
rumination.low: Your answers suggest you rarely get stuck going over the past. When something goes wrong, you seem able to deal with it and then move your attention elsewhere. This is a real strength, because it frees up energy for the present. Keep using what works for you, such as talking things through once or doing something active after a setback. Just make sure you still take a moment to learn from mistakes rather than skipping past them entirely.
rumination.mid: Your answers suggest that past events sometimes keep circling in your mind, especially after stressful days. You can usually let go eventually, but it may take longer than you would like. A helpful step is to notice the difference between problem-solving and simply repeating a thought. Ask yourself: am I getting closer to an answer? If not, try a short distraction, such as a walk or a task that needs focus. Writing your thoughts down once can also help you close the loop.
rumination.high: Your answers suggest you often dwell on the past, replaying mistakes or problems without finding relief. This can drain your energy, disturb your sleep and lower your mood over time. It is a common pattern and it can change. Try setting a fixed, short worry time each day and postponing thoughts until then. Physical activity and absorbing tasks can interrupt the loop. If rumination is affecting your mood, sleep or daily life, a qualified professional such as a psychologist can help you learn effective techniques.

future_worry.name: Future worry
future_worry.short: How much you worry about what might happen next.
future_worry.low: Your answers suggest you face the future with a fair amount of calm. You seem to trust that you can deal with problems as they come, without rehearsing every possible outcome. This makes it easier to enjoy the present. Keep balancing this ease with sensible planning for important matters, such as money or health, so that your relaxed attitude stays well grounded.
future_worry.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes worry about the future, particularly when much is uncertain. Some of this worry may help you prepare, but part of it probably costs more energy than it returns. Try sorting each worry into two groups: things you can act on and things you cannot. Take one small step on the first group. For the second, practise noticing the worry and gently bringing your attention back to what you are doing right now.
future_worry.high: Your answers suggest that worries about the future take up a lot of your attention. You may often picture worst-case scenarios, feel tense about uncertainty or struggle to relax. This kind of worry is exhausting, even when nothing bad happens. Try writing down a worry and then asking how likely it really is and how you would cope. Breathing exercises and regular movement can calm the body. If worry affects your sleep, health or daily functioning, consider talking to a qualified professional who can help.

indecision.name: Indecision
indecision.short: How hard it is for you to make and stick to choices.
indecision.low: Your answers suggest you make decisions with relative ease. You seem to trust your judgement and accept that a good choice does not have to be perfect. This saves you time and stress. Keep checking that speed does not come at the cost of care on big decisions: for major choices, it can help to sleep on it once or ask one trusted person for a second view.
indecision.mid: Your answers suggest that some decisions cost you more time and energy than necessary. You probably decide easily in some areas but get stuck in others, especially when the stakes feel high. Try setting a deadline for each decision and limiting your options to two or three. Remind yourself that most choices can be adjusted later. Aiming for good enough instead of the best possible option often brings more peace with no real loss.
indecision.high: Your answers suggest you often find it hard to make choices and stick with them. You may compare endlessly, ask many people for advice or keep reopening settled decisions. This can lead to missed chances and a lot of mental fatigue. Practise on small decisions: give yourself two minutes and then commit. Write down why you chose, so you can revisit your reasons instead of the whole decision. If indecision is linked to strong anxiety or affects your wellbeing, a qualified professional can help you work through it.

social_replay.name: Social replay
social_replay.short: How much you go over social interactions and what others think of you.
social_replay.low: Your answers suggest you rarely replay social moments afterwards. You seem to take conversations at face value and move on without much second-guessing. This makes social life lighter and more enjoyable. Keep in mind that an occasional moment of reflection can still be useful, for example after a difficult talk, to check whether something needs a follow-up or an apology.
social_replay.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes go over conversations and messages in your head, wondering how you came across. This is very common, especially after new or important encounters. When you notice yourself replaying a moment, ask what evidence you actually have that something went wrong. Remember that most people are busy thinking about themselves. Limit rereading messages to once and then put your phone away.
social_replay.high: Your answers suggest you often replay social interactions and worry about what others think of you. This can make meetings, messages and gatherings feel tiring and can hold you back from connecting with others. Try to catch harsh interpretations and look for a kinder, more realistic explanation. Ask a trusted friend for a reality check now and then. If social worry strongly affects your mood or makes you avoid people, a qualified professional can help you build more confidence in social situations.

summary: Overthinking can show up in different ways: looking back, looking ahead, getting stuck on choices or replaying social moments. Below you see how often each pattern appears in your answers. Higher scores mean the pattern shows up more often. This is a self-reflection tool, not a diagnosis.
